title: Pythia: A Customizable Hardware Prefetching Framework Using Online Reinforcement Learning
authors: Bera, Kanellopoulos, Nori, Shahroodi, Subramoney, Mutlu
relevance: The canonical learned-RL prefetcher: an online contextual-bandit/RL agent that picks prefetch offsets from program context and is rewarded by prefetch quality under current memory-bandwidth utilization. This is exactly the class of learned microarchitectural controller Bouncer must bound — its dynamic, performance-coupled policy is the kind of unverified learned controller that needs a safe-fallback floor and competence auditing.

title: Back to the Future: Leveraging Belady's Algorithm for Improved Cache Replacement
authors: Jain and Lin
relevance: Hawkeye: a learning-based last-level-cache replacement policy that trains a PC-indexed predictor to imitate the offline-optimal Belady (MIN) decisions reconstructed from past accesses. A foundational learned cache controller whose accuracy can drift across workload phases — a prime target for runtime competence auditing against a simple fallback (e.g. LRU/RRIP) floor.

title: Applying Deep Learning to the Cache Replacement Problem
authors: Shi, Huang, Jain, Lin
relevance: Glider: distills an offline attention-LSTM model of cache reuse into a hardware-cheap integer-SVM (ISVM) online replacement predictor indexed by PC history. Demonstrates the offline-train / online-deploy pattern whose deployment-time behavior can diverge from training — motivating Bouncer's set-dueling + CUSUM monitoring of a learned controller versus a fallback floor.

title: Self-Optimizing Memory Controllers: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
authors: Ipek, Mutlu, Martinez, Caruana
relevance: The seminal RL-based DRAM scheduler: an online RL agent learns memory-command scheduling to maximize long-term performance, adapting to dynamic workload state. The earliest learned microarchitectural controller of this family; its long-horizon, hardware-deployed RL policy is precisely the kind of agent Bouncer aims to keep above a safe-fallback scheduling floor at runtime.

title: Dynamic Branch Prediction with Perceptrons
authors: Jimenez and Lin
relevance: Introduces the perceptron branch predictor, the first dynamic branch predictor built on a neural network, exploiting long histories with linearly-scaling hardware. A canonical learned microarchitectural predictor and the lineage Bouncer's learned-controller framing builds on; its per-branch online learning illustrates accuracy that varies by program region.

title: A Case for (Partially) TAgged GEometric History Length Branch Prediction
authors: Seznec and Michaud
relevance: TAGE: the geometric-history-length tagged predictor that remains the state-of-the-art branch-prediction substrate and a multi-time championship winner. As the dominant learned/adaptive branch predictor, it anchors the family of online-trained microarchitectural controllers whose competence Bouncer bounds against a simpler baseline predictor floor.

title: Adaptive Insertion Policies for High Performance Caching
authors: Moinuddin K. Qureshi, Aamer Jaleel, Yale N. Patt, Simon C. Steely Jr., Joel Emer
relevance: The origin of set dueling: dedicate a few sampled sets to each of two competing insertion policies (LRU vs. BIP) and let the winner drive the follower sets via a single saturating PSEL counter. This is the direct architectural ancestor of Bouncer's secret set-dueling design, which uses the same dedicated-sets-plus-counter mechanism to compare a learned controller against a safe fallback floor at near-zero hardware cost.

title: High Performance Cache Replacement Using Re-Reference Interval Prediction (RRIP)
authors: Aamer Jaleel, Kevin B. Theobald, Simon C. Steely Jr., Joel Emer
relevance: Introduces RRIP/DRRIP: a scan- and thrash-resistant replacement family whose Dynamic variant (DRRIP) uses set dueling to choose between SRRIP and BRRIP at runtime. DRRIP is the canonical strong baseline a competence auditor like Bouncer must bound against, and its set-dueling-based policy selection is the mechanism Bouncer generalizes into a safety floor.

title: Adaptive Insertion Policies for Managing Shared Caches
authors: Aamer Jaleel, William Hasenplaugh, Moinuddin K. Qureshi, Julien Sebot, Simon C. Steely Jr., Joel Emer
relevance: Extends DIP/set dueling to shared multi-core caches with the Thread-Aware Dynamic Insertion Policy (TADIP), running an independent set-dueling decision per application thread. Directly relevant to how Bouncer must scope per-context competence monitoring when one shared learned controller serves multiple co-running workloads.

title: Utility-Based Cache Partitioning: A Low-Overhead, High-Performance, Runtime Mechanism to Partition Shared Caches
authors: Moinuddin K. Qureshi, Yale N. Patt
relevance: Establishes the set-sampling / auxiliary-tag-directory monitor methodology that set dueling later distilled: track a small sampled subset of sets to estimate the marginal benefit of a resource allocation at low storage cost. Bouncer's secret-set monitoring inherits this sampling-monitor lineage for low-overhead online competence estimation.

title: Sampling Dead Block Prediction for Last-Level Caches
authors: Samira Manabi Khan, Yingying Tian, Daniel A. Jiménez
relevance: Canonical sampling-based dead-block predictor (SDBP): learns per-PC dead-block behavior from a small sampler of sets using partial tags, achieving high accuracy with far less state than full-cache predictors. The sampler design is the template for cheap, learning-based microarchitectural predictors that a runtime auditor like Bouncer must supervise and bound.

title: SHiP: Signature-Based Hit Predictor for High Performance Caching
authors: Carole-Jean Wu, Aamer Jaleel, William Hasenplaugh, Margaret Martonosi, Simon C. Steely Jr., Joel Emer
relevance: Combines RRIP with a learned signature-based hit predictor (SHCT indexed by PC/memory-region/instruction-sequence) to set insertion priority, and still relies on set-dueling-style mechanisms. A representative learned-predictor-augmented replacement policy that defines the competence target a controller-bounding auditor like Bouncer is meant to track without regressing below a safe floor.

title: The Evicted-Address Filter: A Unified Mechanism to Address Both Cache Pollution and Thrashing
authors: Vivek Seshadri, Onur Mutlu, Michael A. Kozuch, Todd C. Mowry
relevance: Uses a Bloom-filter of recently evicted addresses plus periodic clearing and BIP to jointly fight pollution and thrashing, and dynamically selects behavior in the spirit of set dueling. Relevant to Bouncer as an example of a lightweight online filter that gates a learned insertion decision, mirroring how a CUSUM-monitored auditor gates a controller against a fallback.

title: RETROSPECTIVE: Adaptive Insertion Policies for High-Performance Caching
authors: Moinuddin K. Qureshi, Aamer Jaleel, Yale N. Patt, Simon C. Steely Jr., Joel Emer
relevance: The authors' own 50-years-of-ISCA retrospective on DIP and set dueling, documenting its industrial adoption and limitations in hindsight. Useful framing for Bouncer's motivation: it articulates why cheap online policy-selection mechanisms (set dueling) became standard and where they fall short, which is the gap a formal competence-bounding auditor targets.

title: Using Simplicity to Control Complexity
authors: Lui Sha
relevance: The foundational statement of the Simplex architecture: a simple, formally-verified safety controller plus a decision module bound the behavior of an unverifiable high-performance controller. This is the direct conceptual ancestor of Bouncer's design — a learned uarch controller running on top, dropped to a safe-fallback floor whenever a runtime monitor detects danger. Sha's 'use simplicity to control complexity' framing is exactly the worst-case-vs-baseline guarantee Bouncer enforces in hardware.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning via Shielding
authors: Alshiekh, Bloem, Ehlers, Könighofer, Niekum, Topcu
relevance: Canonical 'shielding' paper: a correct-by-construction shield, synthesized from a temporal-logic safety specification, sits between the RL agent and the environment and overrides any action that could violate safety, while leaving the agent otherwise free to learn. This is the policy-correction analogue of Bouncer's runtime competence audit — the shield provides the hard worst-case floor that the learned controller cannot cross.

title: A Comprehensive Survey on Safe Reinforcement Learning
authors: García, Fernández
relevance: The standard survey that organizes safe RL into worst-case, constrained, and risk-sensitive criteria, and surveys safe-exploration methods including baseline/teacher guidance. Useful for Bouncer to position its 'bound a learned controller to a safe-fallback floor' guarantee within the established taxonomy (worst-case criterion enforced at runtime rather than at training time).

title: Constrained Policy Optimization
authors: Achiam, Held, Tamar, Abbeel
relevance: CPO is the first general-purpose policy-search algorithm with near-constraint-satisfaction guarantees at every iteration, operationalizing the constrained-MDP formulation for deep RL. It is the canonical reference for trading off performance against a cost-constraint budget — directly relevant to how Bouncer reasons about a learned controller that must stay within a bounded competence/safety envelope.

title: Constrained Markov Decision Processes
authors: Eitan Altman
relevance: The foundational monograph defining constrained MDPs and their LP/Lagrangian solution theory — the formal substrate underlying essentially all constrained and safe-baseline RL. Bouncer's notion of bounding a controller subject to a safety/competence constraint inherits directly from Altman's CMDP feasibility-and-optimality machinery.

title: High Confidence Policy Improvement
authors: Thomas, Theocharous, Ghavamzadeh
relevance: Provides a batch-RL algorithm that returns a new policy only when it can guarantee, with user-specified confidence, that the policy's performance exceeds a baseline lower bound — the canonical 'never ship a policy worse than the baseline' result. This is the statistical-guarantee analogue of Bouncer's runtime floor: only deviate from the safe fallback when the deviation is provably (here, high-confidence) at least as good.

title: Safe Policy Improvement with Baseline Bootstrapping
authors: Laroche, Trichelair, Tachet des Combes
relevance: SPIBB falls back to the data-collecting baseline policy precisely on the state-actions where uncertainty is high, and only deviates where the data supports improvement — coming with a formal safe-policy-improvement guarantee relative to the baseline. This 'bootstrap to the safe baseline under uncertainty' mechanism is the algorithmic mirror of Bouncer's set-dueling/CUSUM gate that reverts a learned uarch controller to the safe-fallback floor when its competence is not established.

title: Safe Model-based Reinforcement Learning with Stability Guarantees
authors: Berkenkamp, Turchetta, Schoellig, Krause
relevance: Extends Lyapunov stability verification to learned dynamics so the agent can safely expand its region of attraction while never leaving a certified-safe set. Provides the control-theoretic version of a 'safe region you cannot exit' — relevant to Bouncer as the formal counterpart of a runtime floor that guarantees the system stays within a verified-safe operating envelope while the learned controller explores.

title: A Lyapunov-based Approach to Safe Reinforcement Learning
authors: Chow, Nachum, Duenez-Guzman, Ghavamzadeh
relevance: Constructs Lyapunov functions that guarantee constraint satisfaction during both training and deployment within the CMDP framework, yielding policies that provably stay feasible at every step. This 'safety guaranteed throughout, not just in expectation at convergence' property is exactly the runtime-assurance posture Bouncer needs: the learned controller's actions are admissible only inside the Lyapunov-/floor-defined safe set.

title: Continuous Inspection Schemes
authors: E. S. Page
relevance: The origin of the CUSUM statistic, which is the exact detector Bouncer runs over its secret set-dueling competence signal to flag when the learned uarch controller drifts below the safe-fallback floor. CUSUM accumulates log-likelihood-ratio increments and triggers at a threshold, giving Bouncer a memory-light, single-statistic change alarm.

title: Procedures for Reacting to a Change in Distribution
authors: G. Lorden
relevance: Establishes the asymptotic optimality of Page's CUSUM under the worst-case expected-detection-delay (Lorden's E[T]) criterion subject to a mean-time-to-false-alarm constraint. This is the theory that lets Bouncer claim near-minimal detection latency for competence regressions while bounding nuisance fallbacks, i.e. the formal delay-vs-false-alarm tradeoff governing how fast it bounces a degraded controller.

title: Optimal Stopping Times for Detecting Changes in Distributions
authors: George V. Moustakides
relevance: Proves CUSUM is exactly (not just asymptotically) optimal under Lorden's criterion for i.i.d. observations with known pre- and post-change distributions, via optimal-stopping theory. Justifies Bouncer's choice of CUSUM over ad hoc thresholding: for a given tolerated false-bounce rate, no detector reverts a sub-floor controller sooner.

title: Sequential Analysis: Tests and Confidence Intervals
authors: David Siegmund
relevance: Canonical reference for average-run-length (ARL) computation and the renewal/Wald-approximation theory behind it. Bouncer sizes its CUSUM threshold to hit a target ARL-to-false-alarm; Siegmund's corrected-diffusion and renewal-theoretic ARL approximations are the tools used to translate a tolerable spurious-fallback budget into a concrete detector threshold.

title: Sequential Analysis: Hypothesis Testing and Changepoint Detection
authors: Alexander Tartakovsky, Igor Nikiforov, Michèle Basseville
venue: Chapman & Hall/CRC Monographs on Statistics and Applied Probability
relevance: The modern, comprehensive monograph unifying quickest changepoint detection (CUSUM, Shiryaev-Roberts), ARL/expected-delay theory, and false-alarm constraints. Serves as Bouncer's standing reference for the non-Bayesian quickest-detection framing of online competence monitoring and for variants (e.g. Shiryaev-Roberts) worth contrasting against the deployed CUSUM detector.

title: A Baseline for Detecting Misclassified and Out-of-Distribution Examples in Neural Networks
authors: Dan Hendrycks, Kevin Gimpel
relevance: The reference baseline for out-of-distribution detection via softmax-confidence statistics, framing per-input competence as a monitorable scalar. Bouncer's competence signal is conceptually a streaming OOD/confidence score; this paper anchors the per-example detectability of inputs on which a learned controller is operating outside its trained regime.

title: Algorithmic Learning in a Random World
authors: Vladimir Vovk, Alexander Gammerman, Glenn Shafer
relevance: Foundational text on conformal prediction, which yields distribution-free, finite-sample validity guarantees on prediction reliability under exchangeability. Relevant to Bouncer as the principled way to attach calibrated, assumption-light confidence to the learned controller's outputs and to detect when exchangeability (and thus competence) breaks down at deployment.

title: Distribution-Free Predictive Inference for Regression
authors: Jing Lei, Max G'Sell, Alessandro Rinaldo, Ryan J. Tibshirani, Larry Wasserman
venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association (JASA)
relevance: Develops split/full conformal prediction for regression with finite-sample marginal coverage atop any black-box predictor. This is the practical mechanism by which Bouncer can wrap a learned uarch controller in calibrated prediction sets cheaply enough for online use, turning coverage violations into a monitorable competence signal feeding the change detector.

title: A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation
authors: João Gama, Indrė Žliobaitė, Albert Bifet, Mykola Pechenizkiy, Abdelhamid Bouchachia
relevance: The standard taxonomy of concept-drift detection and adaptation in deployed learners, including drift detectors that are themselves sequential change tests on a streaming error signal. Directly frames Bouncer's problem: detecting when a deployed controller's input/target relationship has shifted enough to warrant reverting to the safe fallback, and the detect-vs-adapt design space around it.

title: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
authors: Stephan Rabanser, Stephan Günnemann, Zachary C. Lipton
relevance: Empirically benchmarks dataset-shift detectors (two-sample tests on learned representations, BBSD, domain classifiers), finding pretrained-feature two-sample testing most reliable. Directly informs how Bouncer should construct and dimensionally reduce its competence signal so that shifts which actually harm the learned controller are detected loudly rather than failing silently.

title: Cache Attacks and Countermeasures: The Case of AES
authors: Dag Arne Osvik, Adi Shamir, Eran Tromer
relevance: The foundational Prime+Probe paper: an unprivileged spy primes cache sets and measures eviction to recover AES keys. It establishes the access-driven contention primitive whose behavioral signature (timing variance from cross-process cache pressure) is exactly the kind of microarchitectural anomaly a runtime competence auditor like Bouncer must distinguish from a learned controller's benign exploration.

title: FLUSH+RELOAD: A High Resolution, Low Noise, L3 Cache Side-Channel Attack
authors: Yuval Yarom, Katrina Falkner
relevance: Canonical Flush+Reload attack exploiting shared (deduplicated) memory and clflush timing on the inclusive L3 to leak victim memory-line accesses at high resolution. It is the reference cross-core leakage primitive whose detectable footprint a runtime auditor would model; Bouncer's set-dueling/CUSUM machinery is conceptually adjacent to detecting the periodic probe cadence such attacks impose.

title: Last-Level Cache Side-Channel Attacks are Practical
authors: Fangfei Liu, Yuval Yarom, Qian Ge, Gernot Heiser, Ruby B. Lee
relevance: Demonstrates a practical cross-core, cross-VM Prime+Probe on the LLC without shared memory, building eviction sets against the slice-hashed last-level cache. This is the canonical cloud-relevant contention attack and a key threat model for any controller (prefetcher/replacement) that Bouncer audits: the learned policy's cache footprint must not become an exfiltration covert channel.

title: Flush+Flush: A Fast and Stealthy Cache Attack
authors: Daniel Gruss, Clémentine Maurice, Klaus Wagner, Stefan Mangard
relevance: Introduces a stealthy attack that times clflush alone (no loads), producing far fewer cache hits/misses and evading performance-counter-based detectors. Directly motivates Bouncer's design tension: a competence auditor relying on coarse hardware-counter signals can be blinded by stealth variants, so its CUSUM-based floor must be robust to low-footprint adversarial behavior.

title: Prefetch Side-Channel Attacks: Bypassing SMAP and Kernel ASLR
authors: Daniel Gruss, Clémentine Maurice, Anders Fogh, Moritz Lipp, Stefan Mangard
relevance: First to weaponize software prefetch instructions as a side channel, leaking address-translation timing to defeat KASLR/SMAP. Central to Bouncer's premise that a learned prefetcher controller is a security-sensitive surface: the same prefetch machinery being tuned for performance can leak addresses, so bounding the controller to a vetted safe-fallback floor is a security as well as performance argument.

title: Adversarial Prefetch: New Cross-Core Cache Side Channel Attacks
authors: Yanan Guo, Andrew Zigerelli, Youtao Zhang, Jun Yang
relevance: Exploits PREFETCHW coherence-state timing to build cross-core Prefetch+Reload / Prefetch+Prefetch channels with record single-line covert-channel capacity. The most direct prior art that a prefetch controller can be an adversarial attack surface, sharpening Bouncer's motivation for keeping any learned prefetcher provably bounded to a safe baseline rather than free to amplify coherence-state leakage.

title: BranchScope: A New Side-Channel Attack on Directional Branch Predictor
authors: Dmitry Evtyushkin, Ryan Riley, Nael B. Abu-Ghazaleh, Dmitry Ponomarev
relevance: First fine-grained attack on the directional branch predictor (distinct from BTB attacks), recovering branch directions by colliding predictor state with the victim. A canonical example of a learned/adaptive microarchitectural predictor being adversarially manipulated, directly paralleling Bouncer's threat model of a learned controller whose internal state can be steered or poisoned and therefore must be fenced by a fallback floor.

title: Jump Over ASLR: Attacking Branch Predictors to Bypass ASLR
authors: Dmitry Evtyushkin, Dmitry Ponomarev, Nael Abu-Ghazaleh
relevance: Shows BTB collisions leak branch target addresses to defeat kernel and user ASLR, the canonical branch-target-buffer attack on an adaptive predictor. Reinforces Bouncer's case that performance-driven learned predictors carry exploitable secret state; a runtime auditor that bounds the controller to a safe floor limits how much an attacker can read out of that learned state.

title: Hey, You, Get Off of My Cloud: Exploring Information Leakage in Third-Party Compute Clouds
authors: Thomas Ristenpart, Eran Tromer, Hovav Shacham, Stefan Savage
relevance: The seminal co-tenancy paper: maps EC2 placement, forces co-residence with a target VM, then uses shared-cache contention to leak keystroke timing. Establishes the cloud co-tenant interference threat model that makes a runtime competence auditor like Bouncer meaningful in shared datacenter hardware where a learned controller's contention behavior is observable by neighbors.

title: Robust Website Fingerprinting Through the Cache Occupancy Channel
authors: Anatoly Shusterman, Lachlan Kang, Yarden Haskal, Yosef Meltser, Prateek Mittal, Yossi Oren, Yuval Yarom
relevance: Introduces the cache-occupancy channel: rather than targeting specific sets, it measures whole-cache contention over time and classifies it with machine learning, working even from JavaScript without high-resolution timers. The aggregate-occupancy + ML-classification methodology mirrors Bouncer's CUSUM/statistical monitoring of a controller's competence, and shows occupancy traces alone carry exploitable signal.

title: Adaptive Insertion Policies for High Performance Caching
authors: Qureshi, Jaleel, Patt, Steely, Emer
relevance: Introduces set dueling: dedicate a few sets to each of two competing policies and let the runtime winner govern the rest at near-zero hardware cost. This is the exact low-overhead online A/B mechanism Bouncer adapts to duel a learned controller against its safe fallback, here used for competence auditing rather than policy selection.

title: An Imitation Learning Approach for Cache Replacement
authors: Liu, Hashemi, Swersky, Ranganathan, Ahn
relevance: PARROT trains a model to imitate Belady's oracle for cache eviction, a flagship ML-for-systems controller. Its oracle-imitation accuracy degrades off-distribution, which is precisely the silent-competence-loss failure mode Bouncer detects and bounds against a non-learned fallback policy.

title: SmartChoices: Augmenting Software with Learned Implementations
authors: Carbune et al. (Google)
relevance: Closest production-systems analogue to Bouncer's safety design: a learned contextual-bandit layer that detects inference faults (malformed inputs, infinite predicted rewards, compiler bugs) and safely falls back to a default arm with alerting. Bouncer generalizes this from fault-triggered fallback to continuous competence auditing with a guaranteed performance floor.

title: Heracles: Improving Resource Efficiency at Scale
authors: Lo, Cheng, Govindaraju, Ranganathan, Kozyrakis
relevance: A feedback controller that safely colocates best-effort work with a latency-critical service by continuously monitoring SLO/QoS and clamping isolation knobs to never violate tail-latency targets. This is the canonical 'bound an aggressive optimizer to a safety floor via runtime monitoring' design that Bouncer mirrors for learned controllers.

title: Autopilot: Workload Autoscaling at Google
authors: Rzadca et al. (Google)
relevance: Production ML-plus-heuristic autoscaler explicitly engineered so the learned recommender minimizes resource slack while bounding the risk of catastrophic OOM kills. It is a concrete datacenter case of guarding a learned component against tail-risk failures, the deployment context Bouncer targets.

title: Park: An Open Platform for Learning-Augmented Computer Systems
authors: Mao, Negi, Narayan, Wang, et al.
relevance: The standard benchmark suite for RL-driven systems controllers, and its motivating analysis documents why ML-for-systems policies are brittle and behave differently from RL-for-games (noisy, non-stationary, distribution-shifting workloads). This is the empirical case for runtime competence monitoring that Bouncer provides.

title: Benchmarking Learned Indexes
authors: Marcus, Kipf, van Renen, Stoian, Misra, Kemper, Neumann, Kraska
relevance: Rigorous evaluation showing learned indexes lose their advantage and robustness on datasets lacking local structure / with erratic CDFs, i.e. they fail under data distribution shift. Direct evidence that a learned system component needs an error-bounded fallback, motivating Bouncer's safety-floor guarantee.

title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems
authors: Sculley et al.
relevance: Foundational articulation of why deployed ML components incur hidden, system-level risk: entanglement, hidden feedback loops, undeclared consumers, and silent changes in the external world. It frames the maintenance and trust hazards that a runtime auditor like Bouncer is built to contain.
